> The SDD is the technical **how**, and it ends in a **cut**. It states the architecture the rest of
> the system builds against — derived from the PRD (the *what and why*), the SRS (the system-level
> *what*) and the UXD (the experience) — and it then cuts that architecture into an ordered set of
> **slices, each of which delivers something on its own**. A slice is not itself a unit of work:
> the Principal PM draws one and cuts it into **one or more** 根回し Nemawashi seeds. § 8 states how
> a slice's fields land in them; how many seeds, when a slice is drawn, and what a seed's stations
> reach into are all `<CORE>/roles/loaders/principal_pm_global.md`'s.
>
> **The cut is the point of the document.** Part B states the method — the steps that turn a design
> into contained slices — and Part C is what those steps produce. A reader who needs to know how to
> plan opens § 5. A reader who needs to know what was planned opens § 6.
>
> It is a **living document**, updated in place with versioning: bump the Version line above on each
> material change. When the build contradicts the cut, § 10 records the contradiction before the cut
> is redrawn.
>
> Omit a section only when it genuinely does not apply; do not pad one to fill it.

## Who decides what

<The CTO writes every part of this document. The table below does not say who writes a part; it says
whose call the part is. A part the CPO or the CDO decides is still drafted by the CTO, best-effort,
from the inputs and any answers already in hand. A call that the inputs leave unsettled, or that the
draft needs that seat to confirm, reaches the document through an `SDD_open_issues.md` item carrying
`- **Seat:** cpo` or `- **Seat:** cdo`, and the answer is folded in on the skill's next round. The
table is the standing split; leave it as written. A draft that decides another seat's column on the
CTO's own judgment has found an open issue, not a mandate.>

**The rule every row follows:** a part is decided by the seat that would have to be overruled for it
to be wrong. Where two seats would each be overruled about different clauses of one part, the part is
split by named clause and each clause names its seat. No part is shared — a shared row is an open
question in the shape of an answer.

| § 2 The shape, and what it was chosen over | **CTO** |
| § 3 The parts, and the seams between them | **CTO** |

| § 4 — the experience conditions the UXD binds on every surface | **CDO** |
| § 5 step 1 — the entries themselves | **CPO** |
| § 5 step 1 — that each entry is genuinely observable, not an architecture box | **CDO** |

| § 6 *Rests on*, *Why here in the order* | **CTO** |

| § 6 *Reached when* — the command and its result, and the artifact that must exist | **CTO** |
| § 6 *Traces to* — the PRD section | **CPO** |
| § 6 *Traces to* — the SRS `FR-n` / `NFR-n` / `DR-n` / `C-n` | **CTO** |

§ 8 is decided by nobody — it is left as written. *SDD Review Notes* names the seat whose call it was on every entry.

**§ 10 has no standing deciding seat, deliberately.** A re-cut is written when a cut meets a reality
that contradicts it, and the trigger says whose ground moved: a *Reached when* that cannot be met
belongs to whichever half failed; a slice that turned out to be a fragment is the CPO's, by § 5
step 2; no slice left that can be started is the CTO's, by step 3; an upstream change belongs to the
seat that owns that document. The CTO writes the record, and it names that seat as the one whose
call moved. A standing decider here would have one seat recording another's error as its own
verdict, which is how a correction stops being distinguishable from a drift.

**What each seat must not decide:** the CTO, whether a slice is worth delivering — that is product
value. The CPO, the architecture style, the data model and the seams. The CDO, product scope and the
technical order.

# Part A — What is being cut

<Part A is the design, kept only as far as the cut is made from it. The SRS holds the requirements
and the UXD holds the experience; neither is restated here. A section of Part A that no slice in
§ 6 rests on is padding — cut it.>

## 1. What this design must achieve

The intent this architecture serves is the PRD's: a reader of folders, files and repositories in
which nothing can be changed — "look, don't touch" (`docs/PRD.md` § Purpose) — for a developer
inspecting a working tree they must not disturb, above all one an automated tool or coding agent
is changing as they watch (`docs/PRD.md` § Target Users, the driving scenario). The edge is that
the guarantee *is* the product: "there is no write path to configure away" (`docs/PRD.md` § Why
This). Every choice below serves the three goals the PRD names — inspection without risk,
pick-it-up adoption, no learning curve (`docs/PRD.md` § Goals) — and is measured by its success
metrics (`docs/PRD.md` § Success Metrics): read-only integrity at zero violations, reckoned at
every release; time-to-first-success at or under five minutes on macOS by the README alone; zero
required configuration; and the two immediacy bars, whose numbers are measured from the first
working build.

The terminus is the project's finish line (`system/projects/ka-reader/finish_line.md`), and the cut in § 6
is scoped to it and no further *(the file was `system/projects/ka-reader/agari.md`, and the terminus
the 上がり Agari, until the instance renamed both on 2026-11-03; the live body of this document
follows the rename from v68 and its dated records keep the old name — `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-62.md`
§ 2.1, RN-128)*. Inside done: the v1 surface — the file tree, reading with
highlighting, Git status, live refresh, against a plain folder as against a repository — plus
diffs, commit history, and switching the viewed folder without restarting, always one folder at a
time. Outside done: sidebar search and filter, pane resizing, keyboard navigation, a second
platform, and a front end for agent workflows or inspection services. Done also means public: MIT,
at version 1.0.0 or later, with the README alone taking a stranger to a viewed file of their own
folder, and the read-only bar at zero violations at the closing release as at every release before
it. A design that reaches for an exclusion — a hosted mode, a programmatic surface, an extension
point, several folders at once — is designing past done, and § 6's *Moves toward* holds every
slice to this line. The first public release is not that closing release: it is a beta below
1.0.0, placed by the PRD once the tree and the open file follow the disk and Markdown reads
rendered, and waiting for nothing else — not for the Git view to follow the disk, not for the
theme (`docs/PRD.md` v18 § Scope (In), *The first public release — a beta*); § 6 S-7 carries it
and § 10 RC-8 records the move.

The constraints fixed before any shape was chosen are the SRS's; they are named here, not
re-listed:

- **The read-only bar is absolute and survives a crash.** No write under the viewed folder, no Git
  mutation, no telemetry, no network call during operation — zero violations at every release, a
  single one release-blocking (`docs/SRS.md` NFR-4 – NFR-9, C-2). The no-network half is held
  by the operating system, never by the code: no network entitlement is ever granted, whatever
  granting one would buy — the owner's ruling (`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-8.md` § 5.1), which § 4
  C-R2 answers to. The owner's second ruling holds the same line against the one thing it was
  found to cost: no mach-lookup exception under another name either, so the renderer that could
  not start without one leaves the system WKWebView (`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-9.md` § 1.1,
  2026-09-23). That is a constraint § 2's shape is re-chosen against, and this section names it
  as one; which native view, and what the seams become, is § 2's weighing and never this
  section's — redone under that ruling (§ 2; § 10 RC-3). What the folder holds is displayed,
  never executed (NFR-16); the folder is
  live, untrusted input that the system tolerates and never requires anything of (DR-6).
- **Local, macOS, one folder.** No hosted mode (C-1); macOS only, with a version floor this SDD
  fixes (C-11); exactly one folder per run, found to be a repository's root or not and never asked
  (FR-1, FR-33); the folder an input the shell can swap, never a structural singleton (NFR-12).
- **One way in.** Exactly one acquisition-and-start path — not a build from source, at most one
  named prerequisite, the channel this SDD fixes (C-3); nothing to configure (NFR-14); no
  programmatic surface at all (`docs/SRS.md` § 5.2).
- **The experience the UXD binds on every surface.** One window, one shell (`docs/UXD.md` § 4);
  the view never lies and draws no state it has not observed (UX-I4, UX-I13); every asset ships
  with the tool (UX-I15); a failing item degrades itself and never the shell (UX-I10, UX-I16).

The test this section sets for § 2 — what tells two shapes apart — is four questions. Can a
reviewer *show*, not be told, that no write path to the viewed folder exists? Does the shell
follow a folder another process is changing without blocking on it or writing to it? Can the
viewed folder be swapped without rewriting the viewing surface? Does the whole thing install on a
Mac by one path, in five minutes, from the README? A shape that cannot be checked on those four has
not been chosen against this section.

## 2. The shape, and what it was chosen over

**The forces, before any shape has a name.** Each is answered from this product's own documents;
the fact that grounds it is on the line.

1. **Where change arrives.** Every change the documents foresee is a new *read surface* over the
   same two sources: the diff, the history and the folder switch are the PRD's deferred features
   inside the terminus (`docs/SRS.md` § 3.6 FR-17 – FR-19, FR-22); the highlighting floor grows
   only by PRD revision (FR-8); the immediacy numbers are confessed unset and arrive by SRS
   revision (`docs/SRS.md` § 4.1 NFR-1, NFR-2, RN-4). No foreseen change adds a *capability* — a
   write, a socket, a shell — because every one of those is excluded permanently (`docs/SRS.md`
   § 7 C-1, C-2; § 4.3 NFR-7, NFR-8). So the shape must price a new read surface cheap and a new
   capability visibly expensive — a boundary a reviewer reads, not a convention a reviewer trusts.
2. **What the system talks to.** Two local sources, both read-only, both owned by others and both
   stable: the filesystem and — only at a repository's root — Git's on-disk state (`docs/SRS.md`
   § 5.3; FR-33). No API, no external service (§ 5.2, § 5.3). The one edge the design expects to
   *swap* is the Git-reading mechanism — "through an installed Git or a library is the SDD's call"
   (§ 5.3) — so that edge earns a port; the filesystem edge does not.
3. **Judgment against plumbing.** The system is mostly plumbing — read, project, watch — and its
   rules are *negative invariants*: never write, never connect, never execute what was read, and
   hold all three through a crash (`docs/SRS.md` NFR-4 – NFR-8, NFR-16). The positive rules are
   few and small: the root finding (FR-33), path containment for rendered content (FR-32, NFR-16),
   never draw an unobserved state (`docs/UXD.md` UX-I13, UX-I16), keep the reader's place across a
   refresh (FR-27). A negative invariant is not held by a guarded domain core; it is held by
   *withholding a capability* at a boundary something outside the code enforces. Since the
   owner's two rulings that boundary has a name — the process's own entitlements (§ 1) — and a
   shape that needs a second process the operating system will not start under them (a system
   service that checks the host's network entitlement at its own start, § 10 RC-2) is asking the
   wall for what the wall refuses.
4. **What must be replaceable inside the terminus.** Two things, both live: the viewed folder —
   "an input, not a structural singleton", and the switch is inside done (`docs/SRS.md` NFR-12,
   FR-19; `system/projects/ka-reader/finish_line.md`, first condition) — and the Git mechanism (force 2).
   Nothing else will be swapped before done: not the platform (C-11), and not the view technology
   *again* — it moved once, before any release, when the system WKWebView was found unable to
   start under the wall (§ 10 RC-2, RC-3; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-9.md` § 1.1). That reversal was
   priced "expensive" in this section's first draft and was paid at the cheapest moment it could
   be: one slice scaffolded, nothing shipped. A seam for a second swap would be cost with no buyer.
5. **What the numbers force at runtime.** One machine, one process tree, one folder per run
   (`docs/SRS.md` C-1, FR-1); no network call during operation, none (NFR-8); own state in the
   tool's own data location and never in the folder (FR-21, DR-5); no configuration of any kind
   (NFR-14). And the promise must survive a crash (NFR-4) — which is what turns "the code declines
   to write" into "the operating system refuses the write": only a wall outside the process holds
   through the process dying. One more thing the rulings force: no network entitlement and no
   mach-lookup exception, ever (§ 1; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-8.md` § 5.1; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-9.md`
   § 1.1) — so every process the product runs starts under that profile, and a view whose own
   processes must pass a network check at their start (WebKit's, RC-2) has no process to run in.
   That leaves one process.
6. **What a first slice could prove.** For each candidate below: the smallest build that shows it
   right or wrong is one that opens a folder, shows its tree, reads one file, and has the *wall*
   in place and machine-checked — because the wall is the shape's whole claim — and, since
   RC-2, a window shown to draw *under* that wall: a wall proven on a bundle whose window never
   drew proved nothing a person could use (§ 4 C-I3, the renderer gate). A candidate whose wall
   cannot be checked until the product is whole carries a warning about itself.
7. **What being wrong costs.** Stated per row, below the table.

**The candidates, run against the forces.** Each row is checked against § 1's four questions —
*show* no write path; follow a moving folder without blocking or writing; swap the folder without
rewriting the viewing surface; install by one path in five minutes — and the question that decides
the row is named on it.

| Shape | Right when | Wrong when | Taken? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sandboxed single-process read pipeline** — one process under the App Sandbox with no network entitlement; a Rust library that reads two sources into one in-memory folder model; an AppKit shell that draws the model's projections and holds no I/O of its own, reached across one closed C-ABI seam | The system's rules are negative invariants that must hold through a crash and are held by the process's own entitlements (force 3, force 5); change arrives as read surfaces rather than capabilities (force 1); and what is shown executes nothing — content reaches the view as data a text engine lays out, so no second process is needed to wall a script engine off | Content must be rendered by an engine that executes it — then a view process that can be handed nothing is worth its seam; or the view needs a system service the wall refuses to start | **yes** — it answers § 1's first question with one entitlements file a reviewer reads (`codesign -d --entitlements`) that covers everything the product runs; the second with a watcher and a model that never hold a write; the third with the folder as a value the model is replaced by (§ 3); the fourth with one bundle and no dependency the view brings (§ 4 C-R1, C-R4, C-R6). Taken over the row below on § 10 RC-2 and the owner's (a) (`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-9.md` § 1.1) |
| **Capability-split read pipeline** — the shape this document held to v12 (ADR-0001): the surfaces in a separate renderer process holding *no* filesystem, network or shell capability, reached through a closed command list and one read-only asset scheme | The renderer executes content — HTML, script — so the process that runs it must be one that can be handed nothing; and the operating system starts that process under the wall | The only renderer that fits refuses to start under the wall (RC-2: WebKit's processes check the host's network entitlement at their own start), or the content is data no engine executes — then the second process guards a threat the design no longer has and costs a serialized seam | no — yes until the owner's (a). No native view process exists that would earn the seam: a view that executes nothing has nothing to be walled off from. It returns if a view that executes content *and* starts under the rule ever exists; none is known |
| **Hexagonal** — a domain core behind ports, an adapter at every edge | Many volatile edges owned by others, and a core carrying rules worth guarding from them (force 2, force 3 the other way round) | The edges are two, stable, and owned by Apple and Git, and the core would hold a folder model and no rule (force 2, force 3): every port but one guards nothing | no — insulating a stable edge is ceremony; its one useful port, the Git reader (force 2), is kept inside the taken shape (§ 3 SM-2). It would win only if the agent-workflow front end came inside the terminus and brought its own edges, which the finish line places outside done. *(Since 2026-11-05 this row is also read against `<CORE>/doctrine/engineering/arch_defaults.md` § *The four layers*, the doctrine's default form of this shape; the paragraph after the table, *The four-layer default, declined by name*, meets that default's own reason; RN-126.)* |
| **Layered, one process** — UI over services over a data-access layer | A product whose data layer's generic filesystem and network access is the point | A product whose defining promise is that such access does *not* exist (force 3): not-writing becomes discipline in a layer built to write | no — fails § 1's first question by construction: a reviewer is *told* the data layer never writes; nothing shows it |
| **Rust-native toolkit, single process** — egui, iced, gpui or Slint: widgets the toolkit draws itself over a GPU surface, one language throughout | One language outweighs the platform's look, and the toolkit's dependency tree is one the product can vouch for | The design starts from what a stock Mac already draws — the platform's fonts, its text sizes, its flat list rows (`docs/DESIGN.md` § Overview; `docs/UXD.md` § 9, "the platform's own controls and appearance are the starting point") — and every dependency is a decision reviewed against an allowlist (§ 4 C-R6): a toolkit that rasterises its own text and ships a GPU stack is a second look and the largest tree of any row, brought to the one seat where the design asks for nothing shipped | no — it keeps one language and loses the look the design is drawn from, and it spends the dependency budget where the platform already provides everything |
| **In-process web engine** — WebKitLegacy's `WebView`, or HTML imported through `NSAttributedString` | The CSS design language must be kept byte for byte, and a deprecated API is acceptable | The engine is deprecated (macOS 10.14), it executes content inside the one process the wall covers, and whether it starts and stays offline under the rule is unmeasured | no — the renderer wall gone *and* a script engine in the host: the worst of the two rows above, on an API Apple has retired. (The previous table's row 4, "Native single-process model-view (AppKit / SwiftUI)", is the taken row now; what survives re-expression of the design language is the CDO's finding, RN-53, not this table's) |
| **Local server + browser tab** — the input proposal's "web app" | A hosted or multi-client direction is inside done | A listening socket is a network call during operation, which NFR-8 forbids outright; and the README no longer calls the product a web app (`docs/PRD.md` § Out of Scope, last item) | no — fails § 1's first and fourth questions: a socket is a capability the wall must forbid, and a browser tab is a second thing to install |

**Which side this product falls on, and why.** The four questions § 1 sets are all *structural*:
each asks for something a reviewer can check without trusting the code — and they are now answered
by one boundary rather than two. The process's entitlements — a read-only grant on the chosen
folder, no network, ever — cover everything the product runs, because everything it runs is one
process (§ 4 C-R2). What the previous shape added, a renderer process that could be handed nothing,
guarded a threat this shape does not carry: content reaches the view as data — a tree of typed
nodes, spans, bytes — and the view hands it to a text layout engine, never to an interpreter (§ 3
`markdown-renderer`; § 4 C-D3). The hexagonal shape still answers with more seams than the product
has volatile edges; the layered and web-app shapes still cannot answer the first question; the
Rust toolkit answers all four and loses on the look and the tree; the in-process engine loses both
walls at once. Until v12 this section landed where ADR-0001 stands
(`docs/adr/0001-capability-split-read-pipeline.md`; RN-1); it departs from that record now, on the
forces as the two rulings re-read them, and the departure is surfaced (§ 10 RC-3; § 12; RN-60).

**The four-layer default, declined by name.** `<CORE>/doctrine/engineering/arch_defaults.md`
§ *The four layers* states a default form of the hexagonal row — `domain`, `ports`, `adapters`,
`entrypoints` under the dependency rule, one fake per port in a test-support module and one
contract suite per port — and "binds a product only once that SDD has chosen it". This SDD does
not choose it. The row above declined hexagonal on volatility (forces 2, 3); the default rests on
a different reason — `domain` and `ports` reach no machine, so every unit is testable with fakes —
and that reason does not carry here either. The one machine edge the default would put behind a
port is the filesystem under the granted folder, which is the product's subject and not a
capability it stands off from: `folder-model`'s tests run against folders they make themselves,
which `<CORE>/doctrine/engineering/testing_doctrine.md` § *A unit test hands its unit fakes and
touches nothing real* admits at layer 1 ("no file outside a temporary folder the test makes for
itself"), and the read-only promise is proven on the real filesystem (`checks/read-only.sh`),
where a fake proves nothing. The other two machine edges are already behind seams — Git behind
SM-2's trait, with libgit2 its only importer, and FSEvents behind SM-3's sink, the model receiving
path reports as data — and the core reads no clock (`SystemTime::now` and `Instant::now` appear
nowhere under `crates/ka-reader-core/src` at `ka-reader@2529a42`). Porting `fs-reader` would place
the containment walk — SM-7's one implementation — behind a fake that can pass a path the real walk
refuses, and would re-cut `docs/nfdr.md` QC-8–QC-11, `checks/structure.sh` and the eleven-part
table for a testability the product has. The core has held a containment port since
`ka-reader@71f9f69` — `ContainmentCheck`, defined in `fs-reader`, `FolderContainment` its one
implementation and `SeededContainment` its one fake (§ 3's `fs-reader` row; SM-7) — and the decline
stands beside it, for the building of the walk: `folder-model`'s entry points build
`FolderContainment` themselves (`crates/ka-reader-core/src/folder_model.rs:L182`, `:L230`, `:L1057`,
`:L1248`, `:L1318` at `ka-reader@98aaa71`), and so does `crates/ka-reader-bridge`, over the held
folder's root, for the two calls that take no model — `asset_bytes` and the relative link
(`crates/ka-reader-bridge/src/session.rs:L1114`, `:L1253`). The port is taken where the check is
handed in — by `markdown-renderer`, by the model's `fill_view` and `reduce_open_file`, and by
`asset_bytes` and `link_file` (SM-5, SM-7). *(Until 2026-11-07 this passage read "for
`folder-model`'s entry points: they call `fs-reader` and build `FolderContainment` themselves
(`folder_model.rs:L181`, `:L229`, `:L991`, `:L1182`, `:L1252`), and `crates/ka-reader-bridge` builds
none" and "taken only where the check is handed in — by `markdown-renderer`, and by the model's
`fill_view` and `reduce_open_file`" — true at `71f9f69`, before the bridge's image-and-link change;
`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-68.md` § 5.2; RN-151. The reads those entry points make are the subject of
*One read seam beside the decline*, below; RN-154.)* What keeps "one implementation" true is
structural, not the contract suite: a release build compiles no implementor of the trait but
`FolderContainment`, because the fake sits behind `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "testing"))]`
(`src/fs_reader.rs:L16-L17`), `testing` is in no default feature and is turned on only by the
crate's dev-dependency on itself (`Cargo.toml`, `[features]` and `[dev-dependencies]`); every
production construction of the check at `98aaa71` is `FolderContainment` — seven, the five in the
model and the two in the bridge named above *(five at `71f9f69`, none in the bridge; RN-151)*; and
SM-7's own rule stands — a node built wrong still reaches no byte, because
`asset_bytes` asks the real check again on every call. The suite
(`crates/ka-reader-core/tests/containment.rs`) proves only that the fake answers as
`FolderContainment` does for the contract's cases; `SeededContainment::seeded` takes any answer for
any reference (`src/fs_reader/fakes.rs:L36-L40`), so a test can seed a pass the real walk refuses.
*(Added 2026-11-07, confirmed in the CTO's seat with the draft's reason replaced;
`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-67.md` § 2.1; RN-148.)* What binds the dependency direction instead is
`docs/nfdr.md` § 1.2's per-part graph, both directions stated and verified by
`checks/structure.sh` — tighter than the default's table, whose `adapters` row admits "the
libraries that reach the machine" where QC-9 forbids the core any Apple framework or a binding to
one (`docs/nfdr.md:L408`). Two things ride with the no. The verified-fake rule attaches to a port,
not to the layer choice (`testing_doctrine.md` § *A fake is verified against its port's contract*
names no layer default), so it reaches two ports today: SM-2's Git port — SM-2 and § 11 R-1 carry
it — and, from `ka-reader@71f9f69`, `fs-reader`'s containment port, `ContainmentCheck` — the
`fs-reader` row and SM-7 carry it *(the second port added 2026-11-07; from 2026-11-05 the sentence
read "so it reaches SM-2's Git port today"; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-67.md` § 2.1; RN-148)*; and it
reaches a third, SM-1's read seam, once that seam is built (*One read seam beside the decline*,
below; RN-154). And
`docs/nfdr.md` § 1.2 gains nothing from this paragraph: `arch_defaults.md`'s layer-recording
sentence binds a product that chose the layers, and § 1.2 already states its graph both ways.
*(Added 2026-11-05. The hexagonal row's words and the sentence "The hexagonal shape still answers
with more seams than the product has volatile edges" were written before the default stood and
stand as written; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-61.md` § 5.1; RN-126.)*

**One read seam beside the decline.** The decline stands for the filesystem as the subject:
listings, bytes, the containment walk and the read-only promise are proven on real folders the
tests make, which `<CORE>/doctrine/engineering/testing_doctrine.md` § *A unit test hands its unit
fakes and touches nothing real* admits at layer 1, and `checks/read-only.sh` proves on the real
filesystem; porting `fs-reader` whole stays declined for the three reasons the paragraph above
gives. One thing a real folder cannot prove for every runner is a **failed read**: `root` ignores a
file mode, so a case that forces a failure with mode `0o000` proves nothing when `root` runs it
(`testing_doctrine.md` § *A test reads nothing of the machine it runs on*, "Who runs it"). At
`ka-reader@98aaa71`, 37 lines in 13 files under `crates/` set that mode on a path a test then reads,
walks past or writes under (`git grep -c '0o000' -- crates`, the per-file counts summed; among them
`crates/ka-reader-core/tests/markdown.rs:L403`, the unreadable bitmap `asset_bytes` refuses), and
the model's reads have no door a test can hand a failing reader through: `folder-model` calls
`fs-reader`'s reads as free functions — `open_root`, `list`, `read`, `observe_file`,
`reobserve_file`, `observe_listing`, `locate`, `locate_parent`, `read_contained_bytes`
(`crates/ka-reader-core/src/folder_model.rs:L79`, `:L102`, `:L183`, `:L232-L233`, `:L287`,
`:L848`, `:L1022`, `:L1041`, `:L1058`, `:L1065`, `:L1070`, `:L1199`, `:L1211`, `:L1249`, `:L1317`).
`fs-reader` itself already reads through two private traits for its own cases — `OpeningFilesystem`
(`src/fs_reader.rs:L55-L59`) and `Filesystem` (`:L238-L246`) — so the form is not new to the
crate; what is missing is the door the model is handed. So this SDD states one read seam beside
the decline, and SM-1 takes its form: a trait defined in `fs-reader` — the readers import nothing
from the model, the reason SM-2's cell gives for the Git port — with one production implementation,
`fs-reader`'s real reads; one fake in the test-support module beside `SeededContainment`, under the
same `cfg` gate, so a release build compiles one implementor; and one contract suite over both at
layer 2, the real run inside a folder the test makes (`testing_doctrine.md` § *A fake is verified
against its port's contract*). The real reader is handed to the model's entry points from the
composition roots — the bridge's session and § 4 C-I3's in-process harness — as the Git port is:
the Rust packet's "a unit is given its collaborators through a trait"
(`<CORE>/doctrine/engineering/languages/rust/conventions.md`) taken for this edge. **What stays
outside the seam answers the paragraph's own objection to a filesystem port:** the containment walk
— `ContainmentCheck`, `FolderContainment` — is not behind it. The walk decides which path may be
read and the seam decides what a read of an admitted path answers, so a fake reader can fail or
refuse an admitted read and can never admit a path the real walk refuses; `FolderContainment` keeps
being built where it is, because a real walk on a readable folder the test makes proves the same
for every runner, and a failed read is the one case that needs a door. The adapter's own failure
path — the real reader at layer 2 — is proven by a condition every runner sees, named by the change
that builds it, never by a file mode. **What this moves, and what it does not.** QC-8, QC-9, QC-11,
`checks/structure.sh` and the eleven-part table do not move: the trait is `fs-reader`'s, no part is
added, and the model still imports `fs-reader`. `docs/nfdr.md` QC-10's setting-aside of the packet
line for the model's edge into `fs-reader` loses its ground for the reads by its own bound (3)
(`docs/nfdr.md:L456`) and narrows to the building of `FolderContainment`, which this paragraph
keeps; that re-opening is the Principal Architect's, on that record's own companion. Once the seam is
built, every case whose failed read crosses SM-1 hands its unit a failing reader,
and no such case forces the failure with a mode; the real reader's own failure cases are proven at
layer 2 by a condition every runner sees, as the sentence above says; and `git grep '0o000'` over
the files the building change names prints nothing. At `98aaa71` those files are eight, holding 23
of the 37 lines: `crates/ka-reader-core/src/folder_model.rs` (2), `tests/list_tree.rs` (4),
`tests/failure_log.rs` (4), `tests/watch.rs` (6), `tests/markdown.rs` (1), `tests/unit/fs_reader.rs`
(4), and the bridge's `tests/open_file.rs` (1) and `tests/open_diagnostics.rs` (1) — each reaching
`fs-reader` through the model's entry points (`open_folder`, `list_tree`, `asset_bytes`:
`folder_model.rs:L78`, `:L101`, `:L278`) or testing the reader itself. One of the 23 is not a read:
`tests/unit/fs_reader.rs:L613` locks a link's target outside the root to prove the walk answers
`Outside` without touching it, the same guard as `tests/tree_links.rs:L95`; the building change
re-states it all the same, because the reader's own suite is that change's and the guard holds for
every runner with a target that does not exist, so the file-level grep holds. **The other 14 lines,
in 5 files, sit where the seam cannot reach, and this paragraph promises nothing about them.**
Twelve are the Git adapter's — `tests/git_state.rs` (7), `tests/root_finding.rs` (4),
`tests/unit/libgit2.rs` (1) — locking a path libgit2 reads, such as `S/.git/config`
(`git_state.rs:L1526`) or `repo/.git` (`root_finding.rs:L177`), and calling the real port;
`git-reader` imports nothing from `fs-reader`, so no SM-1 reader can be handed to it, and the
model-side cases already have SM-2's fake. One is the containment walk's, `tests/tree_links.rs:L95`,
outside the seam by this paragraph's own rule. One is a write, not a read:
`crates/ka-reader-bridge/src/log_writer.rs:L419` seals the log's directory to prove a failed write
is silent. Each of the 14 forces its failure with a mode and proves nothing when `root` runs it — a
known defect at `98aaa71`, under the rule this paragraph already states for the adapter's own
failure path: proven by a condition every runner sees, named by the change that re-states each. No
second seam is cut for them: the Git adapter's twelve are SM-2's adapter-side layer-2 cases, the
walk's guard needs no door because its assertion is `Outside`, and the write is not a read, which
this seam never covers. None of the three is the seam change's. The counts are the pin's. The seam
is **design at `98aaa71`, not code**: the trait's name and methods, and whether it arrives as a
generic parameter or a trait object, are the change's. *(Added 2026-11-07, confirming the lean of
`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-68.md` § 5.5 in the CTO's seat; RN-154. Until the same day's later fold the
grep sentence read "every case that forced a failed read with a mode hands it a failing reader
instead and `git grep '0o000' -- crates` prints nothing; the count above is the pin's" — false by
the 14 lines; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-69.md` § 2.1; RN-156.)*

**The view is AppKit, and its language is Swift.** Two ways draw AppKit: Swift, Apple's own
language for it, or Rust through the `objc2` bindings. Rust would keep the product to one language,
and it costs: every message send is `unsafe` in a workspace that forbids it (`Cargo.toml`,
`[workspace.lints.rust]`), TextKit and `NSOutlineView` are driven through bindings written for a
different idiom, and the contributor who knows AppKit knows it in Swift. Swift costs a second
language beside Rust — the count this product already carried with TypeScript — and one C ABI
between them (§ 3 SM-4); it buys the platform's own controls, and it brings nothing to the tree:
`Package.swift` declares no dependency (§ 4 C-R6). SwiftUI is not taken for the view: the reading
panel is a text view with attachments and block layout (`docs/UXD.md` UX-I12), which is TextKit's
through `NSTextView`, and a SwiftUI layer over it would add a second layout system for no surface
that needs one. The Principal Architect's log records the previous runtime as ADR-0002
(`docs/adr/0002-tauri-2-rust-host-wkwebview-renderer.md`); this paragraph departs from it whole, and
the departure is surfaced with the shape's (§ 10 RC-3; RN-60).

**Undoing it.** Three reversals, priced separately because they cost differently:

- *Moving the view into a second process* costs the bridge (§ 3 SM-4) re-wired as IPC, and nothing
  else — the folder model, the readers and the harness survive. Cheap in code, and blocked while the
  rule stands for any view whose processes check the host's network entitlement (RC-2).
- *Replacing the view technology* costs every surface rewritten (§ 3 `surfaces`, `mac-shell`); the
  core, the bridge's contract and the harness survive. Expensive — paid once, before any release
  (§ 10 RC-3) — and not foreseen again inside the terminus (force 4).
- *Removing the sandbox* costs one entitlements file — and the wall. That is the one reversal the
  design refuses to make cheap to *forget*: the wall's presence is checked on every build (§ 4
  C-I3), so it cannot go missing without a red build saying so.

## 3. The parts, and the seams between them

<The components the system is made of, what each owns, and — as load-bearing — what each must not
own. Then the seams: every place two parts meet, what crosses, and which side owns the contract.
A seam with no named owner is where the design will be argued about later.

**Both tables are read by a tool, not only by a person.** The skeleton launcher creates one
directory per part before any code exists, and it does that by reading the parts table with nothing
in the loop to interpret it. That is why the shape below is fixed rather than left to the run: prose
carries the same content, but no two documents shape it the same way, and a reader that has to
interpret gives a different answer twice over the same settled text. Leave both tables as written.>

**The parts.**

| Part | Lives in | Owns | Must not own |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fs-reader` | crates/ka-reader-core | Listing a folder's entries and reading a file's bytes, each returning its outcome as data (bytes, or the condition observed); the text rule — bytes decode as UTF-8, with or without a byte-order mark, or begin with a UTF-16 byte-order mark and decode as UTF-16, and the file is text; otherwise it is *cannot-display-as-text* (`docs/SRS.md` FR-10) — no encoding is detected from content, no third encoding is admitted, one undecodable sequence makes the file not text, and an empty file is text (the owner's value, RN-41); the extension map that names a floor language or *plain* (FR-29; the set is § 4 C-I5); the **containment check** — after percent-decoding, the path is walked position by position from the granted folder: at every position *inside* the grant the canonical form is taken, symlinks resolved, and the walk goes on from it; at a position *outside* the grant nothing is read — no `lstat`, no `realpath` — and names are compared as spelled, the walk re-entering the grant only on the folder's own name met from its parent position: as spelled, or in another letter case where the folder is not the root of its volume and that volume ignores letter case, both read from the folder itself — never two names the volume keeps apart, and as spelled wherever it cannot be sure; a walk that ends inside the grant is contained and one that does not is refused — run before any open, for every path derived from content or from outside. Three spellings are refused as outside although they may lead in, because proving it would take a read outside the grant (§ 4 C-D1): a path that leaves by more than one level and returns in another case, a Unicode-normalization difference (§ 11 R-10), and a granted folder that is the root of its volume (the owner's answer, `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-15.md` § 5.1; RN-71); the check is reached through a **port**, `ContainmentCheck` — one method, `check(folder, reference) -> Result<ContainedEntry, Condition>` (`crates/ka-reader-core/src/fs_reader.rs:L446-L448` at `ka-reader@71f9f69`), exported from `lib.rs` with `ContainedEntry` and `FolderContainment` — of which `FolderContainment` is the walk's one implementation and `SeededContainment` (`src/fs_reader/fakes.rs`) the port's one fake: it implements the trait and walks nothing, answers `Missing` for any reference not seeded (`fakes.rs:L49-L58`), is compiled under `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "testing"))]` alone (`src/fs_reader.rs:L16-L17`; `testing` is in no default feature and is turned on only by the crate's dev-dependency on itself, `Cargo.toml` `[features]` and `[dev-dependencies]`) and is exported under that feature alone (`lib.rs:L18-L19`); one contract suite, `crates/ka-reader-core/tests/containment.rs`, runs against both *(the port stated 2026-11-07; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-67.md` § 2.1; RN-148)* | Any write. Git, in any form. Watching. Markdown. Deciding what a change means |
| `git-reader` | crates/ka-reader-core | The **Git port** — `probe(folder)` answering `root` or `plain` with discovery disabled and never a path above the folder (FR-33); on a root only, `state()` (branch or detached identifier, the short status word), `status()` (changed and staged entries), `diff(kind, path)` and `walk(tips, window)` (beyond v1) — every method read-only and returning plain data — and its one adapter, libgit2 built with its `https` and `ssh` features off (§ 4 C-R6). The installed-`git` adapter, run with `--no-optional-locks`, is the port's standing substitute and is not built ahead of the risk that needs it (§ 11 R-1). **With the machine-level config off** (the `core-bridge` row's switch) the reader sees two things differently from `git status` in a terminal. The user's global ignore file is not applied, so a file it hides there is listed here as untracked (`libgit2-sys 0.18.8+1.9.7`, `libgit2/src/libgit2/attrcache.c:L345`: the fallback is found through the same search path). And a repository the current user does not own fails to open, because the `safe.directory` entry that would allow it is read from those levels (`repository.c:L629-L634`, `:L1172-L1173`); it is a `failed` Git item. Both follow from `docs/fdr.md` R-101 as it stands — "The product reads nothing outside the viewed folder except its own data location on the machine" (`docs/fdr.md:L188`) — and honouring either means a read outside the grant, which is the owner's to allow (`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-22.md` § 2.1; RN-87). **The config check, run before libgit2 opens anything** (§ 11 R-16; RN-99). Before the probe's open, and before the open behind `state()` and `status()`, the adapter reads every config file libgit2 would load for the repository: the repository's `config` in the common directory; `config.worktree` in the Git directory, where `extensions.worktreeConfig` is set; and every file one of those includes whose path spells to a location inside the folder, the working tree included, to libgit2's own include depth of ten. It refuses the repository where any of them, under a key in § 11 R-16's domain, names a path that spells to a location outside the folder, or carries a value in one of the two forms the adapter refuses without locating (§ 11 R-16, *The spellings*; RN-101). `git-reader` makes these reads itself, with the spelling walk it already locates the Git directory by; the walk follows `fs-reader`'s containment rule and reads nothing at a position outside the folder. Each file is read only for those keys, and under a size bound. A file over the bound, an include depth over ten, or a link chain over the walk's bound is refused. Nothing the check reads reaches the model, the bridge or the log. The refusal answers a condition of its own, on the probe and on both reads, and the condition states which of two things the adapter observed: that the repository's config names a path that spells to a location outside the folder, or that it names a path the adapter does not locate. For the second it does not say *outside* (§ 11 R-16, *The refusal and its condition*; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-36.md` § 5.1; RN-101). It carries which of the two was observed, beside the key and the path as the config spells them, as the condition for an outside Git directory carries its path (§ 11 R-3), and the log line still holds no path. It is not the read-failed condition, which reports a read that was tried, because here none is tried. A config the adapter cannot read answers the existing condition for an unreadable Git directory. A config it cannot parse to the end as Git's syntax answers the existing read-failed condition, because it cannot prove what libgit2 would follow. **The alternates check, run where the config check runs** (§ 11 R-16; RN-100). On the probe, and before the open behind `state()` and `status()`, the adapter reads `objects/info/alternates` under the common directory and refuses the repository where any entry spells to a location outside the folder. `git-reader` makes this read itself, with the same spelling walk and the same size bound as the config check. A link at `objects`, `info` or `alternates` whose spelling leaves the folder is refused without a read. The adapter then reads the `info/alternates` file of each alternate that spells inside the folder, because an inside alternate can name an outside one, to libgit2's own depth of five. A chain deeper than five, a file over the size bound, or a link chain over the walk's bound is refused. The entry spellings are § 11 R-16's. Nothing the check reads reaches the model, the bridge or the log. The refusal answers a condition of its own, and not the config condition, and the condition states which of two things the adapter observed: that the repository's object store names a location outside the folder, or that it names a location the adapter does not locate — an entry beginning with neither `.` nor `/`, which the adapter refuses without locating. For the second it does not say *outside* (§ 11 R-16, "A third way out", *The condition*; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-38.md` § 5.3; RN-103). It carries which of the two was observed, beside the entry as the alternates file spells it, and the log line holds no path. It is built at `ka-reader@6d3ef53`, whose tree outside `docs/` is `ka-reader@0909fe0`'s: the adapter answers `ObjectStoreNotLocated` for an entry whose class is not-located, before spelling any location (`crates/ka-reader-core/src/git_reader/libgit2.rs:L350-L353`), and `ObjectStoreNamesOutside` for an entry spelled outside (`:L358-L360`), on the probe, on both reads and for a submodule (§ 11 R-16, "A third way out", *Built, and the cases that hold it*; RN-105). *(Until 2026-10-07 this sentence said that at `ka-reader@66f428d` the adapter answers one condition for both observations, which § 11 R-16 states as a known defect until a change lands. `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-40.md` § 5.1; RN-105.)* No alternates file, a file holding only empty lines and comments, and an entry that spells inside the folder with nothing there all pass; the last does not reach an entry the adapter does not locate, which is refused whether or not anything is there (RN-103). An alternates file the adapter cannot read answers the existing condition for an unreadable Git directory (`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-35.md` § 2.1; RN-100). **Before the status read, the adapter verifies each submodule repository that read can open**: each gitlink entry of the index whose folder holds a `.git` entry, and each one nested under it, to a stated depth. Three checks run on each, all against the opened folder: its Git directory and its common directory are located by spelling (§ 11 R-3), its config is checked as above, and its alternates file is checked as above (RN-100). Where a submodule fails any of them, `status()` answers the condition observed, and a depth past the bound is refused. Status is never run with that submodule left out, because the list would then read as whole (`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-34.md` §§ 5.1 – 5.4; RN-99). **The `.gitmodules` check, run after the open and before the status read, and on no other call** (§ 11 R-16; RN-102). libgit2 loads `.gitmodules` from the working tree as a config file during the status read (`libgit2-sys 0.18.8+1.9.7`, `libgit2/src/libgit2/submodule.c:L665`, `:L2252-L2255`). Before that read the adapter reads `.gitmodules` in the working tree of the repository and of each submodule it verifies, and every file one of them includes whose path spells to a location inside the folder. `git-reader` makes these reads itself, with the config check's spelling walk, size bound and include depth. Each file is read for two things and for nothing else: its include keys, and each submodule section's path, which is the section's `path` value or, where the section has none, the section's name. An include path is spelled from the directory of the file that carries it, and a section's path from the working tree that holds the file (§ 11 R-16, *The sixth member*). The adapter refuses the status read where either spells to a location outside the folder. It refuses a section's path beginning `/` without locating it. These refusals answer the config condition, with the key and the path as the file spells them and with which of its two observations was made. **The status read reports each gitlink from the repository at that gitlink's own path, and it opens no repository the adapter has not verified.** The adapter refuses the status read where a section of `.gitmodules` would make libgit2 open, or report, another location for a path that read looks up (§ 11 R-16, *The status read and the submodule map*). That refusal answers a condition of its own, and not the config condition: `.gitmodules` gives a submodule path the status read looks up another location. The condition carries the section's name and its path as the file spells them, and the log line holds no path. Nothing either check reads reaches the model, the bridge or the log. A `.gitmodules` the adapter cannot read, for any reason but its absence — the read not permitted, a link, not a regular file, or over the size bound — answers a condition of its own, `GitmodulesUnreadable`, on `status()` alone, and a file a `.gitmodules` includes that cannot be read keeps the existing condition for an unreadable Git directory (§ 11 R-16, *Not covered, and named so it is not read as coverage*, under *The sixth member*; RN-106). That condition crosses SM-2, SM-4 and SM-8 as the config condition does, carries no value, and the shipped sentence for it names no Git directory. *(Until 2026-10-07 this sentence said such a file answers the existing condition for an unreadable Git directory, as built, which § 11 R-16 named as a limit. `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-37.md` § 2.1; RN-102; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-41.md` § 5.2; RN-106.)* All three refusals are built at `ka-reader@1d5c3cf`, whose tree outside `docs/` is `ka-reader@772c63b`'s, the merge that landed them: the adapter answers `ConfigNotLocated` for a section path beginning `/` (`crates/ka-reader-core/src/git_reader/libgit2.rs:L343-L345`), `ConfigNamesOutside` for one spelled outside the folder (`:L346-L349`), and `SubmoduleElsewhere` for a looked-up name whose path spells to another location than the name's own (`:L350-L357`), on the repository's `.gitmodules` and on each verified submodule's, on `status()` alone (`:L100-L104`; `state()` calls `open_verified` alone, `:L96-L98`) (§ 11 R-16, *The sixth member*, *Built, and the cases that hold it*; RN-106). *(Until 2026-10-07 this sentence said that at `ka-reader@5f3e895` the check was built for the include keys alone and the other two refusals were not, which § 11 R-16 stated as a known defect until a change lands. `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-37.md` § 2.1; RN-102; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-41.md` § 5.1; RN-106.)* | Any mutating call — checkout, index write, ref update, lock file. Spawning a process. The model. A file outside Git's own on-disk layout, other than a config file inside the folder that the repository's config includes (RN-99), the `info/alternates` file of an alternate object directory inside the folder (RN-100), and `.gitmodules` in the working tree of the repository and of each submodule the adapter verifies, with the files it includes inside the folder (RN-102) |
| `watcher` | crates/ka-reader-bridge | One FSEvents subscription on the granted folder, the root's `.git` entry included; its native binding and stream lifetime; delivering owned, coalesced path reports to the sink the composition root supplies (SM-3). The native subscription and binding stay inside this part | Reading content. Interpreting a filesystem change. Importing `folder-model` or another part. Any write |
| `folder-model` | crates/ka-reader-core | The in-memory model of exactly one folder (FR-1): the tree, the selection and expansion, the open file, the Git state where the root finding says `root` and none where it says `plain`; every read held as an item carrying an `ItemState` (§ 4 C-I1); the **reducer** that applies reader results and watcher events and keeps the reader's place (FR-27); **the reader's place — the expanded set, the selection, and the open file's path and reading position — is the reader's acts and never a read of the disk, and a delta carries it as it was** (`crates/ka-reader-core/src/folder_model.rs:L405-L407`, `reduce` at `:L772`, at `ka-reader@8ef8c5b`; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-48.md` § 5.2; RN-113). When a delta reports the entry an act names removed, the model keeps the act, inert: it is drawn nowhere, because the parent's listing no longer lists the entry (`reduce_listing`, `:L795-L815`) and a surface draws only from listings; when an entry returns at that path, the held flag or selection binds to it again. A collapse or an expand of a path that no longer resolves is refused at admission (`admit`, `:L710-L714`; `expand`, `:L716`; `collapse`, `:L732`), so the held flag cannot change while the entry is absent — and no row is drawn for it, so no act of the reader's reaches it; `Select(None)` still clears the selection. **The held *listing* under a removed folder is not the place and is not kept as current:** an entry reported removed drops every held listing at and under its path — the listings, never the place — and an entry reported present at a path the place holds expanded is read in that same invalidation, so the folder returns with its listing fresh or `pending`, never the one held before the removal (`docs/UXD.md` UX-I4; `docs/fdr.md` R-81). **Built at `ka-reader@2529a42`, through `Invalidate` and not `Delta`:** the model's `TreeRequest::Invalidate(PathReports)` (`crates/ka-reader-core/src/folder_model.rs:L423-L427`) re-reads whole every held listing the reported paths cover, drops every listing at and under an entry that is gone, keeps the place, and reads a returned folder afresh; `cargo test --locked -p ka-reader-core --test watch` holds the removal and the return (`test_removal_report_removes_the_folder_and_keeps_expansion_and_selection`, `test_a_returning_folder_shows_a_fresh_listing_not_the_old_one`, `crates/ka-reader-core/tests/watch.rs:L736`, `:L817`). `TreeRequest::Delta` keeps its names-only reduction, and no production code calls it: `folder_model.rs:L764` is its one dispatch, and its callers are tests. *(Until 2026-11-05 the clause before this one read "read in that same delta", and this clause read: "**At `ka-reader@8ef8c5b` the reducer does not do this, a known defect until a change lands:** `reduce` touches only listings whose folder a reported path's parent resolves to (`apply_delta`, `:L669-L705`), so a removed folder's own listing stays, and a folder expanded over `a.rs`, removed and reported removed, then recreated holding `b.rs` and reported present, answers `listing("src")` as `["a.rs"]` with `b.rs` on disk — measured through the public API in a disposable clone, in the CTO's seat (`docs/trail/sdd/self_answer-59.md` § Header) and again in the fold that wrote this clause (RN-113); `follow-the-tree`'s command half holds the case (§ 6 S-5; RC-7)." — true at `8ef8c5b`; `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-61.md` § 5.2; RN-126.)* The open file's own removal is `docs/fdr.md` R-80's and the `FileView` *gone* state's, not this clause's. **The open file's re-read, and the form *gone* is held in — built at `ka-reader@d6bc3a3`** (`docs/trail/sdd/cycle-64.md` § 5.2; RN-137): *gone* is a variant of `FileView` (`FileView::Gone`, `crates/ka-reader-core/src/folder_model.rs:L107-L136`), held as `ItemState::Observed(FileView::Gone)` — observed, not failed, because nothing went wrong: nothing was at the path. Only the re-read of the open file reaches it (`FolderModel::reread_open_file`, `:L1201`; `reduce_open_file`, `:L1241`), when `fs_reader::reobserve_file` answers *absent* (`crates/ka-reader-core/src/fs_reader.rs:L476-L514`): no entry at a step of the path as the reader spelled it, or a non-folder where the path goes on, with no link's target being resolved at that step. Everything else that stops a re-read — a folder at the path, an unreadable or non-regular file, a link whose target is missing, outside the folder, looping or too long — is `failed(condition)`, never *gone*; an open or a selection of a path where nothing is answers `failed` as before; an empty file is *text* with no content, not *gone*. It carries no content. The path and the reading position are the reader's place and are never touched by a re-read; the next re-read that reads the file replaces *gone* or `failed` with the view the content makes, with no message. The re-read is reached over SM-5 — an open whose read a batch overlapped, and an `Invalidate` whose reports cover the open file's path (SM-5 names both routes). The delta: `TreeChanges` carries the open file — path, position, view — when the earlier model held none, or one with another path or another view; a change of position or of resolved location alone is not carried (`:L558-L590`; `changes_since`, `:L821`), so a batch over unchanged bytes delivers no open-file member. **Four physical units carry the eleven parts.** `crates/ka-reader-core` is a Rust library that
imports no Apple framework or binding to one and holds no `unsafe`, so the harness links it without a window;
`crates/ka-reader-bridge` is a Rust static library, the only unit that exports a C ABI and the only
one that holds `unsafe`, and its `watcher` part alone owns the FSEvents binding; `ka-reader-mac` is a Swift package building the app's one executable, the
only unit that imports AppKit, declaring no package dependency and linking `libka_reader_bridge.a`;
`checks` is build-time and never shipped. *No `unsafe`* is said of each crate's own Rust source.
The C that `ka-reader-core` links — the grammar engine (`highlighter`'s row) and libgit2
(`git-reader`'s row) — is compiled in beside that source and is outside the claim (§ 9 TO-2,
TO-11; § 11 R-14; RN-80). The unit set departs from the one ADR-0009 records
(`docs/adr/0009-physical-module-set.md`) — `ka-reader-app` and `ka-reader-ui` leave, `ka-reader-bridge` and
`ka-reader-mac` arrive — and the departure is surfaced, not recorded here (§ 10 RC-3; RN-60); the
`crates/` placement is the owner's ruling for every Rust product in this instance as
`docs/nfdr.md` § 9 carries it (RN-4). Only `git-reader` imports the libgit2 binding, with one
exception: `core-bridge` names it in the composition root's search-path switch and that switch's
test, and nowhere else (the `core-bridge` row; RN-87). `ka-reader-core` still holds no `unsafe`. Only
`own-state` and the bridge's log writer write anything; the readers, the watcher, the highlighter
and the renderer import neither the model nor one another, with two stated edges —
`markdown-renderer` calls `fs-reader`'s containment check, and `highlighter` for a fenced block.
The model calls down to `markdown-renderer` and `highlighter` to fill a `FileView`, and — from
`ka-reader@98aaa71` — to the renderer's bitmap-format test, `is_bitmap`, for `asset_bytes`
(`crates/ka-reader-core/src/folder_model.rs:L18`, `:L284`): a file `asset_bytes` serves is exactly
one the renderer draws as an image, one test with one home, and the model asks it only for a path
the check already admitted (`contained_file` runs first, `:L283`). Neither of the two imports the
model — still the one edge from the model into the two, in that direction only (drafted at RN-64,
confirmed by the owner at `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-11.md` § 2.4 — RN-65; the second call added
2026-11-07, `docs/trail/sdd/cycle-68.md` § 5.3; RN-152).

**Watcher placement and delivery (RC-7).** The watcher lives in the bridge so the core remains
free of Apple APIs and the Swift shell retains C-R7's no-I/O boundary. Putting it in the shell
would make native path traffic cross SM-4; this placement needs no such crossing. The bridge
links the system FSEvents/CoreServices API and its CoreFoundation types inside `watcher` only;
it introduces no Apple binding into the core's dependency graph. The exact native binding is
the implementing design's choice under C-R6's dependency review, never permission to add a
binding to `ka-reader-core`. `core-bridge` calls a platform-neutral watcher interface and imports
no Apple framework itself; the part's must-not column continues to hold. The dependency stays
bridge → core; the core imports neither the watcher nor the bridge.

The composition root supplies a sink receiving owned path batches. `watcher` knows neither
`folder-model` nor its request types; the sink's adapter belongs to `core-bridge` and submits the
paths to the model through SM-5. These are invalidation hints, not claims that a file was created,
deleted or successfully read. The model decides which contained listings and reads to repeat,
including affected expanded descendants and, in `follow-the-file`, the open file, and, in `follow-the-folder`, Git state (RC-8).
Apple documents that events may coalesce at an ancestor and that dropped events require a wider
scan ([FSEvents event handling](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/Darwin/Conceptual/FSEvents_ProgGuide/UsingtheFSEventsFramework/UsingtheFSEventsFramework.html)).
The path-only seam handles uncertain coverage conservatively by reporting the granted root;
the watcher never scans to discover what changed. The model treats a reported directory as
potentially covering its descendants, applies the grant boundary and reads through its readers.
A direct Rust test can supply the same path reports without linking the native watcher.

The composition root owns one subscription for the active grant. It establishes delivery before
reconciling the initial snapshot, serializes model work, rejects reports from a superseded grant,
and stops and drains native callbacks before releasing their context. It calls the shell only
after releasing model locks; the shell marshals the resulting projection delta to the main
thread. Bridge/shell cases must cover replacement, stale delivery and callback lifetime. No
native handle, event flag or raw path report crosses SM-4. The `model_changed` projection does.

<**Part** is a **slug**, and what makes one usable is not cosmetic. **Lowercase letters and digits,
single hyphens between them, and nothing else**, written in backticks — no capital, no space, no
underscore, no dot, and no `__PROJECT__`. The skeleton launcher joins this cell to `Lives in` to make
a real directory, and it uses the cell exactly as written — nothing in this column is substituted. A
cell of any other shape is refused, rather than turned into a directory whose name carries the wrong
characters.

It names *the thing* — `connect-unit`, `cache-reader`, `session-store` — never its position in the
list. A positional label (`P-1`, `C-3`) is what a document reaches for on its own and it fails twice
over: it cannot become a directory name, and renumbering the list silently invalidates every
reference to it. A slug survives a renumbering because it never encoded the number. **That half is
the author's to keep, because no tool can check it:** the launcher refuses `P-1` for its capital, and
a lowercase `p-1` is a well-formed slug it has no grounds to refuse.

**A part slug is not a slice slug.** § 6 gives every slice one too, and § 8's map from a slice's
fields to a seed's sections is keyed on *those*. The two name different kinds of thing — a part is a
component that goes on existing, a slice is a unit of work that lands once and is done — and they
must never be spelled the same. Where a slice delivers one part, give them different words rather
than letting one string mean both; § 8 cannot tell them apart, and neither can a reader six weeks
later.

**Lives in** is the module, package or crate the part belongs to, **written as a bare path and
nothing else** — `app-core`, `src/domain`, `crates/reader`. One value, relative to the product
root, no leading `/` and no `..` in it. Not a sentence, not two options, no backticks, no bold, no
trailing clause: a tool joins this cell to the part's slug to make a real directory, so a cell
reading ``app-core`, behind the **Sync port**`` becomes a directory of that name, punctuation and
all. Where a part's placement genuinely needs explaining, the explanation goes in *Owns* and the
cell stays a path. Leave the cell empty for a part that sits at the product root. This is the one
column in which `__PROJECT__` is substituted, for the package named after the product itself.

It is the column most easily left
out, because a human reader infers it from context a script does not have — and without it nothing
knows where a part's directory goes. On a product with more than one language it carries more still:
it is what says which language's layout this part takes.>

**The units.** One row per distinct value in the parts table's *Lives in* column; parts sharing a
value are inside that unit, not directories beneath it. *Language* is a value from the project
card's `Languages:` line; *Kind* is the word that language's packet uses for a buildable unit.

| Unit | Language | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| `crates/ka-reader-core` | `Rust` | `crate` |
| `crates/ka-reader-bridge` | `Rust` | `crate` |
| `ka-reader-mac` | `Swift` | `package` |
| `checks` | `Shell` | `directory` |

The Swift frame — `Package.swift`, `Sources/`, `Tests/` — lands inside `ka-reader-mac/`, where the
card's own test command goes to find it. *Kind* takes the word the Swift packet uses for a buildable
unit, `package` (`<CORE>/doctrine/engineering/languages/swift/layout.md`, in the registry since
`kensaiapp-dev@3ab2e8553`, 2026-09-23), which is also Swift Package Manager's own word; the frame
was laid out by hand in the slice that landed it rather than by a launcher, and how the package is
laid out inside is the packet's and `docs/nfdr.md` § 9's, not this section's. The project card
carries `Swift` in place of `TypeScript` on its `Languages:` line and the `swift test` half in place
of Vitest in its test command (`kensaiapp-opensource@5b27023`; RN-60, RN-66). `checks` is `directory` because
it builds nothing and is forbidden from being a dependency of any shipped unit; Shell is its
language because the card declares Shell for the `checks/*.sh` harness by name (RN-36).

**The seams.** Each names what crosses and which side owns the contract.

| Seam | What crosses | Owner of the contract |
|---|---|---|
| `SM-1` `fs-reader` ↔ `folder-model` | Down: a path to list or read. Up: the listing, or the bytes with the text rule applied and the floor language named, or the condition observed — always as data, never a panic. **The form the crossing takes, stated 2026-11-07 as design** (§ 2 *One read seam beside the decline*; RN-154): a trait defined in `fs-reader`, with one production implementation — `fs-reader`'s real reads — one fake in the test-support module beside `SeededContainment` under the same `#[cfg(any(test, feature = "testing"))]` gate (`crates/ka-reader-core/src/fs_reader.rs:L16-L17`), answering for a path a test names the bytes or the condition this cell's Up already carries and refusing what is not seeded, and one contract suite over both at layer 2, the real run inside a folder the test makes; the real reader is handed to the model's entry points from the composition roots — the bridge's session and § 4 C-I3's in-process harness — as the Git port is over SM-2. The containment walk stays outside it: `FolderContainment` is built where it is (§ 2; SM-7), and the seam answers what a read of an admitted path returns, never which path is admitted.
